claim: Drosophila melanogaster is equipped with two peripheral olfactory organs: antenna and maxillary palp.
source: The vinegar fly Drosophila melanogaster is equipped with two peripheral olfactory organs, antenna and maxillary palp.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the anatomical features of D. melanogaster.

claim: The antenna is involved in finding food, oviposition sites and mates.
source: The antenna is involved in finding food, oviposition sites and mates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established function of the antenna.

claim: The functional significance of the maxillary palp remained unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the functional significance of the maxillary palp remained unknown.
evidence: This statement in the abstract indicates a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Each MP-OSN type is the sole or the primary detector for a specific compound.
source: We found that each type is the sole or the primary detector for a specific compound, and detects these compounds with high sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MP-OSNs detect their key ligands with high sensitivity.
source: We found that each type is the sole or the primary detector for a specific compound, and detects these compounds with high sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by dose-response data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: MP-OSNs mediate short- and long-range attraction.
source: We next dissected the contribution of MP-OSNs to behaviors evoked by their key ligands and found that MP-OSNs mediate short- and long-range attraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5.

claim: The organization, detection and olfactory receptor (Or) genes of MP-OSNs are conserved in D. suzukii.
source: Furthermore, the organization, detection and olfactory receptor (Or) genes of MP-OSNs are conserved in the agricultural pest D. suzukii.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by GC-SSR data and sequence analysis in Figure 6 and the Results section.

claim: Novel short and long-range attractants could potentially be used in integrated pest management (IPM) programs of D. suzukii.
source: The novel short and long-range attractants could potentially be used in integrated pest management (IPM) programs of this pest species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the abstract about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The antenna is covered with four types of sensilla: basiconic, trichoid, intermediate and coeloconic.
source: The antenna, the main olfactory organ, is covered with four types of sensilla: basiconic, trichoid, intermediate and coeloconic.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The maxillary palp has only three different subtypes of basiconic sensilla.
source: In contrast, the palp has only three different subtypes of basiconic sensilla, each housing two MP-OSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Each basiconic sensillum in the maxillary palp houses two MP-OSNs.
source: In contrast, the palp has only three different subtypes of basiconic sensilla, each housing two MP-OSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: There are overlapping response spectra between MP- and antennal OSNs.
source: Because of the overlapping response spectra between MP- and antennal OSNs (Ant-OSNs) (de Bruyne et al., 1999; 2001) as well as the location of the maxillary palp in close vicinity to the labellum, the main taste organ in flies, a function connected to taste enhancement has been suggested for the MP-OSNs (Shiraiwa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A function connected to taste enhancement has been suggested for the MP-OSNs.
source: Because of the overlapping response spectra between MP- and antennal OSNs (Ant-OSNs) (de Bruyne et al., 1999; 2001) as well as the location of the maxillary palp in close vicinity to the labellum, the main taste organ in flies, a function connected to taste enhancement has been suggested for the MP-OSNs (Shiraiwa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Six types of MP-OSNs express seven different odorant receptors (Ors).
source: However, taste enhancement would be a very general function for six types of MP-OSNs expressing seven different odorant receptors (Ors).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Or71a is expressed in the maxillary palp sensillum pb1B.
source: In our previous work we presented data on the importance of Or71a, which is expressed in the maxillary palp sensillum pb1B, in proxy detection of dietary antioxidants (Dweck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Or71a is important in proxy detection of dietary antioxidants.
source: In our previous work we presented data on the importance of Or71a, which is expressed in the maxillary palp sensillum pb1B, in proxy detection of dietary antioxidants (Dweck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In Manduca sexta, CO2 detection is primarily mediated via maxillary and/or labial palp OSNs.
source: For example, in both the hawk moth Manduca sexta and the African malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae, CO2 detection is primarily mediated via maxillary and/or labial palp OSNs (Thom et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In Anopheles gambiae, CO2 detection is primarily mediated via maxillary and/or labial palp OSNs.
source: For example, in both the hawk moth Manduca sexta and the African malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae, CO2 detection is primarily mediated via maxillary and/or labial palp OSNs (Thom et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Mammals possess several peripheral olfactory organs including the main olfactory epithelium, vomeronasal organ, septal organ and Grueneberg ganglion.
source: Mammals are also known to possess several peripheral olfactory organs. In mouse, e.g., the main olfactory epithelium is complemented with the vomeronasal organ, the septal organ and the Grueneberg ganglion, each having distinct functions (reviewed in Knaden and Hansson, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Each peripheral olfactory organ in mammals has distinct functions.
source: Mammals are also known to possess several peripheral olfactory organs. In mouse, e.g., the main olfactory epithelium is complemented with the vomeronasal organ, the septal organ and the Grueneberg ganglion, each having distinct functions (reviewed in Knaden and Hansson, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The study screened MP-OSNs of D. melanogaster using 52 different complex odor sources containing more than 11,300 chemical compounds.
source: In the present study, we present a systematic electrophysiological examination of MP-OSNs of D. melanogaster using 52 different complex odor sources containing more than 11,300 chemical compounds.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a description of the experimental approach.

claim: None or very few ligands have been identified for the different MP-OSNs prior to this study.
source: Although extensive work has been done on the olfactory sense of the vinegar fly, D. melanogaster, none (e.g. for pb3A-OR59c, Pb2A-Or33c) or very few ligands have been identified for the different MP-OSNs (de Bruyne et al., 1999, Goldman et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Previously identified ligands for MP-OSNs activate Ant-OSNs as well as MP-OSNs.
source: In addition, the previously identified ligands activate Ant-OSNs as well as MP-OSNs and have been shown to be much better ligands for Ant-OSNs (i.e. require high concentrations to activate MP-OSNs) (de Bruyne et al., 1999; Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Previously identified ligands are much better ligands for Ant-OSNs than MP-OSNs.
source: In addition, the previously identified ligands activate Ant-OSNs as well as MP-OSNs and have been shown to be much better ligands for Ant-OSNs (i.e. require high concentrations to activate MP-OSNs) (de Bruyne et al., 1999; Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The study screened each of the six MP-OSNs with headspace collections from 52 different complex, ecologically relevant odor sources using GC-SSR.
source: Towards this end, we screened each of the six MP-OSNs with headspace collections from 52 different complex, ecologically relevant odor sources using GC-SSR (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–6, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures showing the experimental data.

claim: The odor sources included 34 fruits, seven microbes, and eleven types of mammal feces.
source: These odor sources included 34 fruits, seven microbes, and eleven types of mammal feces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental materials.

claim: Each of the tested headspace collections triggered a response from at least one palp OSN type.
source: Our GC-SSR measurements revealed that each of the tested headspace collections triggered a response from at least one palp OSN type.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the GC-SSR experiments.

claim: Fecal, fruit and microbial volatiles elicited responses from six, five and two palp OSN types, respectively.
source: Fecal, fruit and microbial volatiles elicited responses from six, five and two palp OSN types, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the GC-SSR experiments.

claim: The pb2B MP-OSN was activated exclusively by fecal volatiles.
source: The pb2B MP-OSN was activated exclusively by fecal volatiles, whereas the other five types were activated by fruit, microbial, and fecal volatiles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the GC-SSR experiments.

claim: Five MP-OSN types were activated by fruit, microbial, and fecal volatiles.
source: The pb2B MP-OSN was activated exclusively by fecal volatiles, whereas the other five types were activated by fruit, microbial, and fecal volatiles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the GC-SSR experiments.

claim: The 52 headspace collections were separated into three distinct groups: fruit samples, microbial samples and fecal samples.
source: This analysis indicated that the 52 headspace collections were separated into three distinct groups; one group for fruit samples, another group for microbial samples and the last group for fecal samples (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NMDS analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The differences between the three groups (fruits, microbes, feces) were statistically significant (ANOSIM score R = 0.61, p<0.0001).
source: The significance of the differences between these three groups was assessed by the analysis of similarity (ANOSIM) score (R = 0.61, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a statistical analysis of the NMDS results.

claim: The information provided by the different MP-OSNs is sufficient to categorize fruits, microbes, and feces.
source: These results suggest that the information provided by the different MP-OSNs is sufficient to categorize fruits, microbes, and feces.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the NMDS analysis.

claim: The total number of distinguishable FID peaks in the samples was 11326.
source: The total number of distinguishable flame ionization detection (FID) peaks in the samples was 11326, of which only 328 FID peaks elicited responses (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 7, and Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantification of the chemical complexity of the samples.

claim: Only 328 FID peaks elicited responses from MP-OSNs.
source: The total number of distinguishable flame ionization detection (FID) peaks in the samples was 11326, of which only 328 FID peaks elicited responses (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 7, and Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the GC-SSR experiments.

claim: 225 of the physiologically active peaks corresponded to 20 different compounds.
source: 225 of these peaks corresponded to 20 different compounds (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: The identified compounds belonged to four different chemical classes: alcohols, esters, phenols and ketones.
source: The identified compounds belonged to four different chemical classes: alcohols, esters, phenols and ketones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a classification of the identified compounds.

claim: Phenol and 4-methylphenol occurred exclusively in fecal extracts.
source: Phenol and 4-methylphenol occurred exclusively in fecal extracts (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Compounds that activated different MP-OSNs differed in their descriptors and distributed widely in the two-dimensional odor space.
source: In this odor space, odors with similar descriptors mapped close to each other, whereas odors with diverse descriptors distributed widely. Indeed, compounds that activated different MP-OSNs differed in their descriptors and, hence, distributed widely in the two-dimensional odor space.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Compounds that activated the same MP-OSN clustered together except for the ligands recognized by pb2A.
source: Compounds, however, that activated the same MP-OSN clustered together except for the ligands recognized by pb2A (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: pb2A is the only MP-OSN that expresses two olfactory receptors, Or33c and Or85e.
source: This could be explained by the fact that pb2A is the only MP-OSN that expresses two olfactory receptors, Or33c and Or85e (Couto et al., 2005; Goldmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: (-)-fenchone is a previously identified best ligand for Or85e.
source: In order to predict which of these two receptors could detect which of the pb2A ligands, we included (-)-fenchone, a previously identified best ligand for Or85e (Goldman et al., 2005), in our PCA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The responsiveness of pb2A to furaneol methylether was due to the expression of Or33c.
source: This result suggests that the responsiveness of pb2A to furaneol methylether was due to the expression of Or33c, while the responsiveness of pb2A to (-)-camphor, alpha- and beta-ionone was due to the expression of Or85e.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The responsiveness of pb2A to (-)-camphor, alpha- and beta-ionone was due to the expression of Or85e.
source: This result suggests that the responsiveness of pb2A to furaneol methylether was due to the expression of Or33c, while the responsiveness of pb2A to (-)-camphor, alpha- and beta-ionone was due to the expression of Or85e.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only one best ligand was identified for most MP-OSNs except for pb1B and pb3B, where two best ligands for each were identified.
source: Only one best ligand was identified for most MP-OSNs except for pb1B and pb3B, where two best ligands for each were identified (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 2.

claim: The detection threshold of pb1A, pb1B, pb2B and pb3B for their best activators was 10–7 dilution.
source: The detection threshold of pb1A, pb1B, pb2B and pb3B for their best activators was 10–7 dilution, whereas the detection threshold of pb2A and pb3A was 10–6 and 10–4dilution, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 2.

claim: The detection threshold of pb2A for its best activator was 10–6 dilution.
source: The detection threshold of pb1A, pb1B, pb2B and pb3B for their best activators was 10–7 dilution, whereas the detection threshold of pb2A and pb3A was 10–6 and 10–4dilution, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 2.

claim: The detection threshold of pb3A for its best activator was 10–4 dilution.
source: The detection threshold of pb1A, pb1B, pb2B and pb3B for their best activators was 10–7 dilution, whereas the detection threshold of pb2A and pb3A was 10–6 and 10–4dilution, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 2.

claim: The high sensitivity of MP-OSNs suggests that the maxillary palps could be involved in evaluating odor sources over long distance similar to the antennae.
source: This high sensitivity suggests that the maxillary palps could be involved in evaluating odor sources over long distance similar to the antennae.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the sensitivity data.

claim: Four of the best activators of MP-OSNs (5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, and phenol) elicited no response from any of the Ant-OSNs.
source: Four of these best activators (5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, and phenol) elicited no response from any of the Ant-OSNs, while the other four triggered responses from four additional Ant-OSNs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GC-SSR data in Figure 4A.

claim: Four of the best activators of MP-OSNs triggered responses from four additional Ant-OSNs.
source: Four of these best activators (5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, and phenol) elicited no response from any of the Ant-OSNs, while the other four triggered responses from four additional Ant-OSNs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GC-SSR data in Figure 4A.

claim: When odors activated both Ant-OSNs and MP-OSNs, the receptor pairs cluster on a phylogenetic tree, suggesting a shared ancestor.
source: Interestingly, when odors activated both Ant-OSNs and MP-OSNs (4-ethylguaiacol: Or69a and Or71a; 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate: Or67a and Or85d; butyl 3-hydroxy butyrate: Or59c and Or85a) in the latter two cases the receptor pairs cluster on a phylogenetic tree, suggesting a shared ancestor (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Three compounds (4-ethylguaiacol, 2-phenethyl acetate, phenethyl propionate) were primarily detected by the MP-OSNs as the detection threshold for Ant-OSNs was two orders of magnitude higher than for MP-OSNs.
source: Three of the compounds were primarily detected by the MP-OSNs as the 10–5 detection threshold for these Ant-OSNs was two orders of magnitude higher than the 10–7 detection threshold for MP-OSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Butyl 3-hydroxy butyrate was primarily detected by the Ant-OSN ab2B.
source: The fourth activator, butyl 3-hydroxy butyrate, was primarily detected by the Ant-OSN ab2B. The detection threshold of ab2B to this compound was one order of magnitude (10–5 dilution) lower than that of the corresponding MP-OSN pb3A (10–4 dilution).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dose-response data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The MP-OSNs are either the sole or the primary detectors of ecologically relevant concentrations of 5-hexen-3-one, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, phenol, 2-phenethyl acetate, and phenethyl propionate.
source: Together, this data suggests that the MP-OSNs are either the sole or the primary detectors of ecologically relevant concentrations of 5-hexen-3-one, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, phenol, 2-phenethyl acetate, and phenethyl propionate (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the dose-response experiments.

claim: Six out of the eight tested compounds were behaviorally active.
source: Six out of the eight tested compounds were behaviorally active; two compounds, 5-hexen-3-one and furaneol methylether, in T-maze assays, four compounds, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, in trap assays, and one compound, furaneol methylether, in wind tunnel assays (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A.

claim: 5-hexen-3-one and furaneol methylether were attractive in T-maze assays.
source: Six out of the eight tested compounds were behaviorally active; two compounds, 5-hexen-3-one and furaneol methylether, in T-maze assays, four compounds, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, in trap assays, and one compound, furaneol methylether, in wind tunnel assays (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A.

claim: 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate were attractive in trap assays.
source: Six out of the eight tested compounds were behaviorally active; two compounds, 5-hexen-3-one and furaneol methylether, in T-maze assays, four compounds, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, in trap assays, and one compound, furaneol methylether, in wind tunnel assays (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A.

claim: Furaneol methylether was attractive in wind tunnel assays.
source: Six out of the eight tested compounds were behaviorally active; two compounds, 5-hexen-3-one and furaneol methylether, in T-maze assays, four compounds, 4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, in trap assays, and one compound, furaneol methylether, in wind tunnel assays (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A.

claim: Orco[2] mutant flies were not attracted by the behaviorally active compounds.
source: In contrast to WT flies, Orco[2] mutant flies were not attracted by these compounds (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that the flies' behavior displayed to these compounds requires Or genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5B.

claim: The flies' behavior displayed to the behaviorally active compounds requires Or genes.
source: In contrast to WT flies, Orco[2] mutant flies were not attracted by these compounds (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that the flies' behavior displayed to these compounds requires Or genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the Orco[2] mutant data.

claim: Flies are strongly repelled by 5-hexen-3-one, 4-ethylgauaicol, and phenol at 10–2 concentration.
source: We found, indeed, that flies are strongly repelled by 5-hexen-3-one, 4-ethylgauaicol, and phenol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The aversion elicited by 10–2 concentration of 5-hexen-3-one, 4-ethylgauaicol, and phenol was independent of functioning Ors.
source: Interestingly, the aversion elicited by this concentration was independent of functioning Ors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The palp best ligands represent positive cues at lower concentration.
source: From our results we conclude that the palp best ligands represent positive cues at lower concentration, and that the processing of this information requires Or genes, while the processing of higher concentrations seems to be independent of functioning Ors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claim: The processing of information from palp best ligands at lower concentrations requires Or genes.
source: From our results we conclude that the palp best ligands represent positive cues at lower concentration, and that the processing of this information requires Or genes, while the processing of higher concentrations seems to be independent of functioning Ors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claim: The processing of higher concentrations of palp best ligands seems to be independent of functioning Ors.
source: From our results we conclude that the palp best ligands represent positive cues at lower concentration, and that the processing of this information requires Or genes, while the processing of higher concentrations seems to be independent of functioning Ors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claim: For 4-ethylguaiacol, 5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol and furaneol methylether, amputation of the palps resulted in loss of attraction.
source: For 4-ethylguaiacol, 5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol and furaneol methylether, amputation of the palps resulted in loss of attraction, while amputation of the antennae did not affect the behavior (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C.

claim: For 4-ethylguaiacol, 5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol and furaneol methylether, amputation of the antennae did not affect the behavior.
source: For 4-ethylguaiacol, 5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol and furaneol methylether, amputation of the palps resulted in loss of attraction, while amputation of the antennae did not affect the behavior (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C.

claim: For 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, amputation of the palps had no effect on the behavior.
source: Interestingly for 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate amputation of the palps had no effect on the behavior, while amputation of the antennae abolished attraction elicited by these two compounds (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C.

claim: For 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, amputation of the antennae abolished attraction.
source: Interestingly for 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate amputation of the palps had no effect on the behavior, while amputation of the antennae abolished attraction elicited by these two compounds (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C.

claim: Killing pb2A OSNs via expression of hid from Or33c- or Or85e-promoter significantly reduced attraction towards furaneol methylether compared to both parental lines.
source: In wind tunnel experiments, killing pb2A OSNs via expression of hid from Or33c- or Or85e-promoter significantly reduced attraction towards furaneol methylether compared to both parental lines (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 5D.

claim: The maxillary palp of D. suzukii contains three sensillum types as found in D. melanogaster.
source: We found that the maxillary palp of D. suzukii contains three sensillum types as found in D. melanogaster, and that OSN types and their pairing within a particular sensillum type in D. suzukii are the same as in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GC-SSR experiments.

claim: OSN types and their pairing within a particular sensillum type in D. suzukii are the same as in D. melanogaster.
source: We found that the maxillary palp of D. suzukii contains three sensillum types as found in D. melanogaster, and that OSN types and their pairing within a particular sensillum type in D. suzukii are the same as in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GC-SSR experiments.

claim: The detection of D. melanogaster palp best activators is conserved in D. suzukii.
source: In addition, our screen revealed that the detection of these compounds is also conserved in D. suzukii (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GC-SSR data in Figure 6A.

claim: The amino acid sequences of Or genes are well conserved in the D. suzukii genome: Or33c (82.2%), Or42a (90%), Or46a (83.5%), Or59c (78.4%), Or71a (81.4%), Or85d (86.5%) and Or85e (85%).
source: This comparison revealed that the amino acid sequences of these genes are well conserved in the D. suzukii genome: Or33c (82.2%), Or42a (90%), Or46a (83.5%), Or59c (78.4%), Or71a (81.4%), Or85d (86.5%) and Or85e (85%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate are produced by yeast.
source: The yeast producing volatile 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate (Dweck et al., 2015; Christiaens et al., 2014), elicited positive chemotaxis in trap and/or T-maze two-choice assays, while the ripening signal, furaneol methylether (Ulrich et al., 1997), induced positive chemotaxis and upwind attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Furaneol methylether is a ripening signal.
source: The yeast producing volatile 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate (Dweck et al., 2015; Christiaens et al., 2014), elicited positive chemotaxis in trap and/or T-maze two-choice assays, while the ripening signal, furaneol methylether (Ulrich et al., 1997), induced positive chemotaxis and upwind attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Furaneol methylether induced positive chemotaxis and upwind attraction in D. suzukii.
source: The yeast producing volatile 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate (Dweck et al., 2015; Christiaens et al., 2014), elicited positive chemotaxis in trap and/or T-maze two-choice assays, while the ripening signal, furaneol methylether (Ulrich et al., 1997), induced positive chemotaxis and upwind attraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from behavioral experiments.

claim: 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol are fermentation signals produced by the metabolism of hydrocinnamic acids in fruits by yeasts.
source: The fermentation signals produced by the metabolism of hydrocinnamic acids in fruits by yeasts, 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol (Dweck et al., 2015), did not induce any behavioral response in D.suzukii in contrast to D. melanogater.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol did not induce any behavioral response in D. suzukii in contrast to D. melanogaster.
source: The fermentation signals produced by the metabolism of hydrocinnamic acids in fruits by yeasts, 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol (Dweck et al., 2015), did not induce any behavioral response in D.suzukii in contrast to D. melanogater.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from behavioral experiments.
